text: Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.
author: Epictetus
work: Enchiridion, chapter 5
explanation: One way to read this passage: examine the judgement you bring to an event. Your first interpretation can be tested before it guides your response.
example: A colleague hasn’t replied. The late reply is an observation; ‘they’re ignoring me’ is an interpretation. Check that interpretation before acting.
biography: A Greek Stoic philosopher of the first and early second centuries CE, who taught in Rome and later Nicopolis. His teaching focused on ethical judgement and the choices we make.
evidence: Compared chapter 5 in MIT’s Elizabeth Carter translation on 2026-10-09; checked Dickinson commentary and Stanford’s Epictetus entry. Explanation and example are editorial interpretations, not quotations. Public-domain translation.

text: the life which is unexamined is not worth living
author: Socrates, as portrayed by Plato
work: Plato, Apology, 38a
explanation: In Plato’s account of his trial, Socrates treats examining our beliefs and conduct as central to living well. One practical reading is to make room for questioning the reasons behind your choices.
example: Before repeating a familiar routine, ask what it serves and whether that purpose still matters to you.
biography: An Athenian philosopher famous for questioning people about their beliefs. He left no written works; Plato and other ancient writers provide differing portraits of him.
evidence: Exact excerpt compared with MIT’s Benjamin Jowett translation on 2026-10-10. The speaker is Socrates in Plato’s text, not a surviving work by Socrates. Author context checked against Stanford. Public-domain translation.

text: the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
author: Laozi · traditional attribution
work: Daodejing, chapter 64
explanation: The surrounding passage describes large things growing from small beginnings. A practical interpretation is to attend to beginnings while a situation is still manageable, and let progress develop step by step.
example: For a daunting project, choose one concrete first action and give it your attention.
biography: Traditionally credited with the Daodejing, a foundational Daoist text. The historical identity of Laozi and the text’s authorship remain subjects of debate.
evidence: Compared the exact excerpt in chapter 64 of Project Gutenberg’s James Legge translation on 2026-10-10. Preserved ‘li’ rather than replacing it with ‘miles’. Traditional attribution and authorship uncertainty checked against Stanford. Public-domain translation.

text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer.
author: Marcus Aurelius
work: Meditations, book VI, section 6
explanation: A practical reading of this Stoic reminder: someone else’s misconduct need not set the standard for your own response. You can challenge a wrong while preserving your judgement and character.
example: Answer a hostile email with a clear account of the problem and a boundary, without borrowing its insults.
biography: A Roman emperor and Stoic thinker (121–180 CE). The Meditations records personal reflections on duty, judgement and living with other people.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Book VI, sixth reflection; George Long translation, a public-domain translation. Preserved the edition’s wording “wrong doer”. Author/tradition context checked against the linked academic reference. Explanation and example are editorial interpretations.

text: Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
author: Seneca
work: Of the Shortness of Life, section II
explanation: Seneca asks how much of life we actually give to what matters, rather than merely counting its length. One useful reading is to examine the demands that consume your time by default.
example: Before accepting another recurring meeting, ask what it contributes and whether that purpose deserves the time.
biography: A Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and dramatist (c. 4 BCE–65 CE). His essays and letters explore ethical judgement, emotions and the use of time.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Of the Shortness of Life II in Minor Dialogues Together with the Dialogue on Clemency, George Bell, 1889; public-domain Aubrey Stewart translation. text: it is not one swallow or one fine day that makes a spring
author: Aristotle
work: Nicomachean Ethics, book I, chapter VII (1098a)
explanation: In discussing happiness, Aristotle looks at the shape of a whole life rather than a single good day. A practical interpretation is to judge your habits by their sustained pattern, with room for occasional setbacks.
example: Look at how you have treated people over the month, rather than letting one excellent or awkward conversation define you.
biography: A Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose work ranges from logic and biology to ethics and politics. His ethics asks how character and activity contribute to living well.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Exact clause in book I, chapter VII; edition credits D. P. Chase. Public-domain translation. Retained “spring”, not the different “summer” wording found in other translations. Author/tradition context checked against the linked academic reference. Explanation and example are editorial interpretations.

text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
author: Confucius
work: Analects, book XV, chapter XXIII in Legge’s numbering
explanation: The passage offers reciprocity as a guide to conduct: consider the effects of what you impose on others. A practical reading starts with restraint, then asks about the other person’s actual needs.
example: Before sending a late request with a tight deadline, consider how you would receive it and ask what timing is workable.
biography: A Chinese teacher and thinker traditionally dated 551–479 BCE. The Analects gathers sayings and dialogues associated with him; its compilation and interpretation developed over time.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Book XV, CHAP. XXIII, Tsze-kung’s question about a rule for life; public-domain James Legge translation. Used the linked edition’s numbering rather than silently substituting modern XV.24. Author/tradition context checked against the linked academic reference. Explanation and example are editorial interpretations.

text: Once upon a time I dreamt I was a butterfly
author: Zhuangzi · traditional attribution
work: Zhuangzi, chapter 2; “Dream and Reality” selection
explanation: The butterfly dream unsettles the confidence with which we distinguish perspectives and identities. One way to engage with it is to notice how deeply a role or state of mind colours what seems obvious.
example: After a day spent inside one difficult project, step back and ask how the situation looks to someone outside that role.
biography: A Chinese thinker associated with the fourth century BCE and a foundational Daoist text. The Zhuangzi is a composite work; the butterfly dream appears in its Inner Chapters.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Opening clause of “Dream and Reality” in Gems of Chinese Literature, Herbert A. Giles; public-domain translation. Marked as an excerpt and retained traditional attribution. Author/tradition context checked against the linked academic reference. Explanation and example are editorial interpretations.

text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
author: Dhammapada · Buddhist tradition
work: Dhammapada, chapter I, verse 5
explanation: This verse challenges the cycle of retaliation. A practical reading is to respond without adding fresh hostility, while still addressing harm and setting boundaries. “Love” is the wording of this historical translation.
example: When a discussion becomes angry, name the issue calmly and propose a next step instead of returning the attack.
biography: A collection of verses in the Pali Buddhist canon, traditionally understood as teachings of the Buddha. It is a transmitted collection rather than a book written by a single known author.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Chapter I, The Twin-Verses, verse 5; public-domain F. Max Müller translation, Sacred Books of the East X (1881). Preserved the historical translator’s “love”; attributed the collection to Buddhist tradition. Author/tradition context checked against the linked academic reference. Explanation and example are editorial interpretations.

text: Thy business is with the action only, never with its fruits;
author: Bhagavad Gita · Krishna in the dialogue
work: Bhagavad Gita, discourse 2, verse 47
explanation: Krishna distinguishes commitment to action from attachment to its reward. One practical reading is to do your part carefully without demanding a guaranteed outcome; the surrounding verse also warns against inaction.
example: Prepare well for a presentation, then give your attention to delivering it rather than trying to control every reaction.
biography: A Sanskrit philosophical dialogue within the Mahabharata, traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Krishna and Arjuna discuss action, knowledge and devotion; Krishna speaks this verse.

text: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
author: Mary Wollstonecraft
work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, chapter IV
explanation: Wollstonecraft argues for women’s independent judgement and agency. The goal in this passage is self-government, supported by education, rather than replacing one group’s domination with another’s.
example: Help someone build the knowledge to make their own decision instead of making that decision for them.
biography: An English philosopher and writer (1759–1797). She argued that women should receive an education that develops reason and independence, and challenged assumptions about their supposed natural inferiority.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Chapter IV, response to Rousseau on women’s education; public-domain original English (1792). text: If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?
author: Mary Astell
work: Some Reflections Upon Marriage, Appendix, page 150 (1730 edition)
explanation: Astell exposes a tension between claims of natural freedom and women’s enforced subordination. A practical reading is to test whether a principle is being applied consistently to everyone it supposedly covers.
example: If a team promises that everyone has a voice, check whose objections are regularly ignored before celebrating the principle.
biography: An English philosopher (1666–1731) who advocated women’s education and examined marriage and authority. Her arguments about women’s condition were grounded in a strongly Christian philosophy.

text: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
author: John Stuart Mill
work: On Liberty, chapter II
explanation: Mill argues that understanding a position requires engagement with the reasons against it. One practical reading is to meet the strongest opposing argument rather than a convenient version supplied by your own side.
example: Before recommending a plan, write down the best reason a thoughtful colleague might reject it and answer that reason fairly.
biography: An English philosopher (1806–1873), known for work on liberty, utilitarian ethics and logic. His writing examines how open discussion and individuality contribute to human development.
evidence: Compared exact wording with the linked primary edition on 2026-10-10. Chapter II, Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion, passage following the discussion of Cicero; public-domain original English (1859). Preserved the comma after “case”. text: Keep the faculty of effort alive in you by a little gratuitous exercise every day.
author: William James
work: The Principles of Psychology, volume I, chapter IV: Habit
explanation: James recommends small, deliberate exercises of effort as part of forming habits. A practical interpretation is to practise doing useful things that require attention, instead of waiting for the ideal mood.
example: Choose one small task you have been avoiding and finish it deliberately, without turning the exercise into punishment.
biography: An American philosopher and psychologist (1842–1910). His work on mind, habit, experience and religion helped shape pragmatism and modern psychology.

text: Whoso would be a man, must be a nonconformist.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
work: Essays, First Series: Self-Reliance
explanation: Emerson urges readers to exercise their own judgement rather than surrender it to approval or custom. A practical reading values thoughtful independence; it need not mean disagreeing for its own sake.
example: When everyone favours a familiar approach, check whether your own reasons support it before joining the consensus.
biography: An American essayist, poet and philosopher (1803–1882), associated with Transcendentalism. His essays explore self-reliance, education, nature and the changing perspectives of experience.

text: Our life is frittered away by detail.
author: Henry David Thoreau
work: Walden: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For
explanation: Thoreau asks what happens when the demands of daily life crowd out deliberate living. One practical reading is to simplify what you can so that important work, relationships and observation receive real attention.
example: Close a few minor open loops, then protect an uninterrupted hour for something you actually care about.
biography: An American philosopher, naturalist and writer (1817–1862). Walden explores deliberate living, while his political essays examine conscience, government and civil disobedience.

text: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
author: Baruch Spinoza
work: Ethics, part V, proposition XLII, concluding note
explanation: This closes Spinoza’s discussion of freedom and blessedness through understanding. A practical interpretation is that worthwhile clarity may demand sustained effort; difficulty alone does not prove that a pursuit is valuable.
example: Give a recurring emotional pattern time and careful examination instead of expecting one clever insight to resolve it.
biography: A philosopher born in Amsterdam’s Portuguese-Jewish community (1632–1677). His Ethics connects nature, knowledge, emotions and the possibility of human freedom.

text: To know by rote, is no knowledge
author: Michel de Montaigne
work: Essays, book I, chapter XXV: Of the Education of Children (this edition)
translation: Charles Cotton, edited by William Carew Hazlitt · excerpt
explanation: Montaigne distinguishes reciting a lesson from making its meaning your own. A practical reading is to test understanding through explanation and application, rather than treating accurate repetition as enough.
example: After learning a procedure, explain why it works and what you would change if one of its assumptions failed.
biography: A French philosopher and essayist (1533–1592). His Essays use personal experience, reading and sceptical inquiry to exercise independent judgement.

text: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough;
author: René Descartes
work: Discourse on the Method, part I
explanation: Descartes follows this clause by stressing the right application of the mind. One practical reading is to value a careful method for examining a problem, rather than relying on speed or confidence alone.
example: Before acting on a convincing first explanation, identify its assumptions and test one that could change the result.
biography: A French philosopher and mathematician (1596–1650). He developed influential accounts of method, doubt, knowledge and the relationship between mind and body.

text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
author: Francis Bacon
work: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral: Of Studies
explanation: Bacon distinguishes the benefits of reading, discussion and writing. A practical reading is to use each deliberately: encounter ideas, test them in conversation, then write precisely enough to expose gaps.
example: When a decision still feels vague, discuss it with someone and write down the reasons in a few clear sentences.
biography: An English philosopher and statesman (1561–1626). He advocated a reform of knowledge through systematic inquiry and wrote essays on conduct, judgement and public life.
